messages.content: Predict the participant’s recorded human response, without advice, moral evaluation or explanation. You are a child in a candy activity with an experimenter. A covered tray holds a nearer dish with two real wrapped Starburst candies and a farther dish with six. You cannot reach in from above. A short hooked tool reaches only the nearer dish; two short tools joined by a red connector can reach the farther dish. You have been instructed and helped to retrieve the farther dish and now have its six candies. Your own paper bag is brown; the current other child’s bag is marked black. Any candy you keep goes into your bag, promised to you at the end, and any candy you give goes into the other child’s bag. The other child is absent and cannot reject or counteroffer. There is one allocation; no cash conversion or random-one-trial rule is stated. The experimenter turns away to give privacy. Earlier you completed a separate forgiveness task involving a different child with a white-marked bag who used a scratch sheet intended for you. Your decisions in that earlier task are not supplied; that child is not the current black-bag recipient. You may give any whole number g from 0 to 6 candies to the other child and keep 6−g. Output only that integer g.

The experimenter supplied the second tool, without describing another child as providing it or forgoing candies. Only after you retrieved the six candies were you told that a child who could not be here today also likes Starbursts and that you could give some to them. The black-marked bag is for that absent child. How many of the six candies do you put in the other child’s black-marked bag?
Participant background: reported integer age in years 6; boy. Individual race and parental education are not provided.
